title: Why Supreme Court Justices Have to Show Their Books
hook: Federal judges don't campaign for office or face voters — so how does the public keep tabs on their outside income, gifts, and travel? One tool: a legally required annual disclosure.
key_points: Federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, must file annual financial disclosure reports listing income, gifts, travel, and investments.
The requirement exists precisely because judges aren't elected and don't answer to voters directly — disclosure is a substitute check on undisclosed influence.
These reports are public, letting journalists and watchdog groups scrutinize a justice's outside income and potential conflicts of interest.
A 2026 NPR review of the justices' annual reports found that book deals and royalties make up a meaningful share of some justices' income, alongside disclosed gifts and travel.
Disclosure doesn't ban outside income or gifts outright — it trades an outright ban for transparency, on the theory that sunlight lets the public and other branches judge for themselves.
content_html: Elected officials answer to voters; federal judges, deliberately, don't. That insulation is meant to protect judicial independence, but it also removes the most direct check people have on public officials. One of the substitutes for that missing accountability is a legal requirement most people have never heard of: judges, including Supreme Court justices, must file public annual reports disclosing their outside income, gifts, and travel.
extra_html: NPR's Nina Totenberg reviewed the justices' 2026 disclosures and found that book deals and royalties add up to a meaningful part of some justices' income, alongside the gifts and travel the reports are built to surface. The rule doesn't ban outside income or gifts outright — a justice can still write a bestselling book or accept a trip — it simply requires that it all be made public, trusting that transparency itself, rather than a flat prohibition, is enough to let the public and other branches judge whether an arrangement looks like a conflict of interest. (This card describes U.S. federal judicial disclosure rules specifically.)

flashcards.prompt: Why are federal judges required to file annual financial disclosure reports?
flashcards.back_html: Because they aren't elected and don't answer to voters directly, disclosure acts as a substitute check — letting the public see outside income, gifts, and travel that might create conflicts of interest.

flashcards.prompt: What did NPR's 2026 review of Supreme Court financial disclosures highlight?

choices.text: That book deals and royalties make up a meaningful share of some justices' income
That justices are barred from earning any outside income at all
That financial disclosure reports are sealed and unavailable to the public

flashcards.explanation_html: The reports are public precisely so outside income like book royalties can be reviewed and scrutinized.

flashcards.prompt: What's the underlying tradeoff behind judicial financial disclosure rules?

choices.text: They don't ban outside income or gifts outright — they require transparency instead, trusting public scrutiny to catch problems
They ban judges from accepting any gift or outside income whatsoever
They apply only to judges who have been previously investigated

flashcards.explanation_html: Disclosure is a lighter-touch tool than an outright ban — it relies on sunlight rather than prohibition to guard against conflicts of interest.
